text:
Finite energy does not prevent the velocity from sharpening in one part of the fluid.
A nontrivial change can be carried through less and less distance while the total \(L^2\)-size remains bounded.
That shrinking distance is the concentration a singularity would have to exploit.
In three dimensions, vortex stretching is the motion that can drive it.

% !TeX root = ../navier-stokes-manuscript.tex
\subsection{Vortex Stretching}\label{sub:ThePerfectlyStretchingVortex}

The surrounding strain pulls the rotating region along its axis, and the region lengthens.
The condition \(\nabla\cdot u=0\) preserves the volume of every material tube.
If that tube remains tube-like while it stretches, its average transverse area has to decrease.
The contraction need not be the same in both transverse directions.

The vorticity itself is not frozen inside that material tube.
Viscosity continues to diffuse it across the moving particle labels.
The dangerous motion is the coupled one in which strain keeps amplifying the rotation while the vorticity core remains concentrated across smaller transverse widths.
If the velocity difference across that core does not flatten at the same rate, the same variation is being carried through less distance and the spatial gradient grows.
This is the stretching vortex we need to follow.

Write
\[
  \omega:=\nabla\times u,
  \qquad
  S:=\frac12\bigl(\nabla u+(\nabla u)^{\mathsf T}\bigr).
\]
Taking the curl of Navier--Stokes gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:VorticityEquation}
  \partial_t\omega+(u\cdot\nabla)\omega
  =S\omega+\nu\Delta\omega.
\end{equation}
The left side is the material rate of vorticity measured along a moving particle.
When \(\omega\) points along an extensional direction of \(S\), the term \(S\omega\) can amplify it.
Since \(\operatorname{tr}S=\nabla\cdot u=0\), extension in that direction is balanced by net transverse contraction, though not necessarily by equal radial thinning.

Taking the scalar product with \(\omega\) makes the two simultaneous effects exact:
\[
  \frac12(\partial_t+u\cdot\nabla)|\omega|^2
  =\omega\cdot S\omega
  +\frac{\nu}{2}\Delta|\omega|^2
  -\nu|\nabla\omega|^2.
\]
The strain term can increase the vorticity.
The viscous term contains both spatial diffusion and the negative gradient contribution.
At a local maximum of \(|\omega|^2\), its complete pointwise contribution is nonpositive; after integration over the whole space, it gives the usual vorticity dissipation.
Nothing in this identity says that the favourable alignment will persist or that the core will keep concentrating.
It identifies the motion that would have to remain active for the sharpening to continue.

The kinetic-energy law watches the same motion from much farther away:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:BodyEnergyIdentity}
  \frac12\norm{u(t)}_2^2
  +\nu\int_0^t\norm{\nabla u(s)}_2^2\,ds
  =\frac12\norm{u_0}_2^2.
\end{equation}
It controls the total velocity and the time-integrated dissipation.
It does not record the width across which a local velocity change occurs.
The stretching vortex has supplied exactly that missing feature: concentration into a smaller spatial scale.

To measure that concentration, use the full Navier--Stokes scaling.
For \(\lambda>1\), set
\[
  u_\lambda(x,t)=\lambda u(\lambda x,\lambda^2t),
  \qquad
  p_\lambda(x,t)=\lambda^2p(\lambda x,\lambda^2t).
\]
This maps a solution with datum \(u_0\) to a rescaled solution with datum
\[
  u_{\lambda,0}(x)=\lambda u_0(\lambda x).
\]
It compares one normalized profile at different scales; it does not say that the fixed solution evolves by repeatedly rescaling itself.
Every term in the equation acquires the same factor:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \partial_tu_\lambda(x,t)
  &=\lambda^3(\partial_tu)(\lambda x,\lambda^2t),
  &
  (u_\lambda\cdot\nabla)u_\lambda(x,t)
  &=\lambda^3\bigl((u\cdot\nabla)u\bigr)(\lambda x,\lambda^2t),
  \\
  \nabla p_\lambda(x,t)
  &=\lambda^3(\nabla p)(\lambda x,\lambda^2t),
  &
  \Delta u_\lambda(x,t)
  &=\lambda^3(\Delta u)(\lambda x,\lambda^2t).
\end{aligned}
\]
Inside this rescaled family, a spatial width is reduced by \(\lambda^{-1}\), the velocity amplitude is multiplied by \(\lambda\), and the time coordinate is reduced by \(\lambda^{-2}\):
\[
  x\mapsto\lambda^{-1}x,
  \qquad
  u\mapsto\lambda u,
  \qquad
  t\mapsto\lambda^{-2}t.
\]

Scaling now defines the height at which concentration should be measured.
For a homogeneous Sobolev norm,
\[
  \norm{u_\lambda(t)}_{\dot H^s}^2
  =\lambda^{2s-1}
  \norm{u(\lambda^2t)}_{\dot H^s}^2.
\]
Exactly one exponent is unchanged:
\[
  2s-1=0,
  \qquad
  s=\frac12.
\]
With \(\Lambda:=(-\Delta)^{1/2}\), define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:BodyCriticalHeightDefinition}
  H(t)
  :=\frac12\norm{u(t)}_{\dot H^{1/2}}^2
  =\frac12\norm{\Lambda^{1/2}u(t)}_2^2.
\end{equation}
We call \(H(t)\) the critical height because the scaling leaves it standing while the scales around it move.

Under the same transformation,
\[
  \norm{u_\lambda(t)}_2^2
  =\lambda^{-1}\norm{u(\lambda^2t)}_2^2,
  \qquad
  \norm{\nabla u_\lambda(t)}_2^2
  =\lambda\norm{\nabla u(\lambda^2t)}_2^2,
\]
while
\[
  H_\lambda(t)=H(\lambda^2t).
\]
The rescaled profile can carry less kinetic energy and larger derivative size at the same critical height.
This is the gap left open by the energy law: concentration can become more severe without announcing itself through an increase in total kinetic energy.

Applying \(\Lambda^{1/2}\) to Navier--Stokes and pairing with \(\Lambda^{1/2}u\) gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:BodyCriticalHeightBalance}
  H'(t)
  +\nu\norm{\Lambda^{3/2}u(t)}_2^2
  =\mathcal P_{1/2}(t),
\end{equation}
where
\[
  \mathcal P_{1/2}(t)
  :=-
  \operatorname{Re}
  \left\langle
    \Lambda^{1/2}\bigl((u\cdot\nabla)u\bigr),
    \Lambda^{1/2}u
  \right\rangle_{L^2}.
\]
The pressure pairing vanishes here because \(\Lambda\) commutes with spatial derivatives and \(u\) is divergence-free.
The critical height rises only through the signed nonlinear transfer, while viscosity acts through the next spatial derivative.

The scaling has also shortened the time coordinate by \(\lambda^{-2}\).
That number is not the duration of a scale transition produced by the nonlinear solution.
It is the clock on which viscosity responds once a smaller width is present.
